Figure 8. The life cycle the group commits to when it deploys a model: release with the paper, a dependency review every six months, retraining when the source database changes materially, a usage review that watches the fraction of out-of-domain submissions, and an announced end of the maintenance window with the artefact archived under a DOI. The dates are a policy, not a prediction; what matters is that they exist in writing before the tool is published.

Exercise 2

Write the sunset paragraph for a tool your own project would deploy: how long it is maintained, who maintains it after the author graduates, what is archived and where, and what a user should do when the service stops. Then check the last three computational tools you used from a paper: how many are still running, and how many tell you what to do if they are not?

11. Summary

Shipping a model means shipping a contract, not a file: a prediction, an interval with measured coverage, an applicability-domain verdict and evidence a chemist can judge. The same function serves the application and the API, which is what keeps the two consistent.

Serialisation is not documentation. saveRDS() stores an object with no record of the packages that produced it, and in R — a language whose design has always coupled data analysis to the graphics and environment that produced it[3] — it also stores the environment of any function you save — the careless closure measured here carried ten megabytes of an unrelated matrix into the file alongside the model. A manifest with package versions, data checksums, metrics and licences turns a binary into an artefact, and a start-up environment check turns a silent incompatibility into a refusal[5] — the same requirement that reproducibility standards for machine learning in the life sciences place on any published predictor[6].

Validate before predicting. Every rejection class — empty, too long, unparsable, unsupported elements, outside the size window, a mixture, and (in this R build) not featurisable — returns a reason rather than a number or a traceback, and the standardised structure is echoed back so the user sees what was actually scored.

Silent extrapolation is the failure mode of deployment. Asked about decoys and about the most dissimilar chemistry available, the model returned confident-looking potencies whose spread collapsed towards its training mean, while the distance measure flagged them and the prediction itself gave no sign. Within the scaffold test set the same measure barely graded the error at all: a domain flag is a filter on what may be asked, not a correction to the answer.

Model cards and dataset cards are the instrument for that[1][2]: intended and unintended uses, provenance and biases of the data, metrics under the honest split, the domain definition with its threshold, limitations, and a maintenance commitment — generated from the analysis, like everything else in Unit 23.

Deployment creates obligations: secrets from the environment, logs without chemistry, two version numbers, a health endpoint, a watch on the distribution of what users submit, and a written sunset policy with an archived artefact so that the paper outlives the server.

Bridge

The model served here was built in Unit 14, validated on the splits of Unit 12, explained with the attributions of Unit 16, and given its applicability domain and conformal intervals in Unit 17; its data and their biases come from Unit 6, its reporting from Unit 23, the package and tests behind the service from Unit 24, and the container it is deployed in from Unit 25. The capstone, U27, asks for a model card as part of the deliverable. In the sister courses, Validation covers the QSAR reporting conventions a model card must satisfy, Descriptors and fingerprints explains the representation whose bits appear in the attributions, and the R edition of the AI course, Model evaluation, covers the metrics quoted in the card. The Python edition of this unit, which deploys the same model with Streamlit and FastAPI, is here.

12. Self-assessment

  1. A collaborator asks for “the model”. What do you send, and why is the file not enough?

The model file, a manifest (package versions, data checksum, hyperparameters, metrics, split), the inference code including validation and the applicability-domain definition, and the model card. The .rds alone is an object whose behaviour depends on the version of ranger that loads it, and which says nothing about what it was trained on, how well it does on new chemistry, or where it must not be used.

  1. Why must the conformal quantile be computed on a calibration set rather than on the training residuals?

Because a random forest fits its training data almost perfectly, so training residuals are far smaller than prediction errors on new compounds; intervals built from them would be far too narrow. The calibration set is data the model never saw during fitting, which is what makes the rank argument behind conformal validity apply. In the three-way split used here the calibration compounds also share no scaffold with the training compounds.

  1. Work out the conformal index for n = 199 calibration residuals at 95 % confidence, and say what happens at n = 15.

k = ceiling(200 x 0.95) = 190, so the half-width is the 190th smallest of the 199 residuals. At n = 15, ceiling(16 x 0.95) = 16 > 15: the required index does not exist, so a 95 % interval cannot be formed. The rule is n >= 1/eps - 1, that is at least 19 calibration points for 95 %; with fewer, report a lower confidence and say so.

  1. The tool returns a plausible potency for a molecule from an unrelated chemistry. Is the model broken?

No - it is doing what regression models do. A random forest averages the training leaves its input falls into, so an unfamiliar molecule receives something close to the training mean, with no indication that the question was inappropriate. The defect is in the interface if it shows that number without the applicability-domain verdict; in Section 6 every one of the most dissimilar decoys was flagged, at a mean domain distance more than half again the threshold, and that flag — not the number — is the answer the user needs.

  1. Give three input classes your validation must reject and the message for each.

An unparsable string (“unbalanced parentheses: not a parsable SMILES string” - a compound name or a truncated paste is the usual cause); a molecule with unsupported elements (“unsupported elements: Pt” - the training set is small organic molecules); and a structure outside the size window (“about 120 heavy atoms, outside the supported range 3-70”). A mixture or salt is a fourth class, handled differently: the largest fragment is kept and the user is told, because silently predicting for a different species is worse than refusing.

  1. Where does a shiny application load its model, and why not inside the server function?

At the top level of app.R, which runs once per R process and is shared by every session. Loading inside server() would reload the bundle for every user who connects, and loading inside a reactive() would reload it on every input change. The reactive graph is the other half of the answer: one reactive() holds the prediction and every output reads it, so the model is called once per input change regardless of how many outputs there are.

  1. What does FastAPI’s schema give that the plumber service has to do by hand?

Declarative validation before any user code runs, a machine-readable 422 naming the offending field, and an OpenAPI specification generated from the same declaration. plumber has no type annotations to read, so the batch cap, the allowed confidence levels and the type of the smiles field are checked in explicit code — which works, but means the documentation and the implementation can drift apart unless the checks and the annotations are reviewed together.

  1. Which four tests would you write for the API, and what does each protect?

A malformed payload returns 422 (the validation is active); a request without the key returns 401 when a key is configured (the secret is enforced, not merely present); an unparsable structure returns a 200 with status: “rejected” and a reason (one bad molecule does not fail a batch); and a reference molecule returns the same prediction to three decimals (a golden test protecting against an unnoticed model or dependency change). The first three call the handler directly, as Section 8 does; the fourth belongs with the package tests of Unit 24.

  1. A user reports that the prediction for their compound changed between Monday and Friday. How do you diagnose it?

Ask for the model_version from the response they kept, and compare with the current one from /model. If the versions differ, the model was retrained and the NEWS file says why. If they are the same, the environment changed under the service: compare the running package versions with the manifest — which is the check that should have refused to start — and look at the logs for a restart. This is why the version travels in every response.

  1. What belongs in the “not intended” section of a model card for this predictor?

Absolute potency for decisions without experimental confirmation; selectivity against other kinases, which it was never trained on; anything clinical, diagnostic or safety-related; and prediction for molecules outside the stated applicability domain. The section exists because a model is used for whatever it plausibly answers, and the author is the only person who knows what it cannot do.

  1. Your free-tier application has been asleep for three months and the paper is published. What should already be in place?

An archived release of the repository and the model artefact with a DOI, cited in the paper instead of (or alongside) the URL; a README with local installation instructions; a stated maintenance window; and a named contact. The service going to sleep is then an inconvenience rather than a reproducibility failure — which is the practical content of a sunset policy.

  1. A colleague wants to score a 200,000-compound catalogue through your API. What do you tell them?

Not through the API: at the per-compound latency measured in Section 5 the arithmetic alone is of the order of ten minutes of uninterrupted prediction, and as 200,000 separate HTTP calls it is far more; the batch endpoint is capped at 200 structures for exactly that reason. Give them the package and the model artefact so they can run it locally or on the cluster with the parallelisation of Unit 25, and point out that most of those compounds will be outside the applicability domain, so the useful first step is to filter by distance to the training set before predicting anything.

Glossary

Applicability domain
The region of chemical space where a model’s predictions are supported by training data; here, 1 minus the mean Tanimoto similarity to the five nearest training compounds, with a threshold from the training distribution.
Bit ablation
A local explanation for a fingerprint model: the change in the prediction when one set bit is switched off. Cheap, counterfactual, and blind to interactions between bits.
Conformal prediction (inductive)
A distribution-free method giving intervals with a stated coverage, built from the quantile of residuals on a held-out calibration set.
Dataset card / datasheet
A structured description of a data set: provenance, composition, collection process, biases, recommended and discouraged uses, licence.
Environment of a closure
The frame in which a function was defined, saved with it by saveRDS; the reason a one-line function can produce a multi-megabyte file.
Health endpoint
A trivial route (/health) that a hosting platform or monitor polls to decide whether a service is alive.
Model card
A short structured document stating a model’s intended and unintended uses, training data, metrics under a named evaluation, applicability domain, limitations and maintenance.
plumber
The R package that turns annotated functions into HTTP endpoints; validation of the request body is written by hand.
Reactive (shiny)
An expression that recomputes only when its inputs change; the unit of caching in a shiny application.
saveRDS / readRDS
R’s single-object serialisation; records no package versions, and stores the environment of any function it is given.
Silent extrapolation
A confident-looking prediction for an input outside the model’s domain; detectable only by a domain check, never by the prediction itself.
Sunset policy
The written commitment describing how long a deployed tool is maintained, what is archived, and what users should do when it stops.
testServer
shiny::testServer(): drives a server function’s reactive graph in-process, so an application’s logic can be tested without a browser or a port. 
produced <- sort(basename(list.files(TMP, pattern = "rock1_rf|manifest|CARD|closure")))
cat("artefacts written by this document:", paste(produced, collapse = ", "), "\n")
## artefacts written by this document: DATA_CARD.md, MODEL_CARD.md, closure_bad.rds, closure_good.rds, manifest.json, rock1_rf_v1.0.0.rds
invisible(file.remove(list.files(TMP, pattern = "rock1_rf|manifest|CARD|closure", full.names = TRUE)))
cat("artefacts removed:", length(list.files(TMP, pattern = "rock1_rf|manifest|CARD|closure")) == 0, "\n")
## artefacts removed: TRUE

In a real deployment those files are the release: the .rds, the manifest, the two cards and the application source, tagged in the repository and archived under a DOI. Here they were written into the session’s temporary directory and deleted, because a document that leaves artefacts behind is a document that will one day be run twice.
